### 3.2.1 Genealogical and Epistemological Dimensions

The genealogy of dark patterns in interface design originally stems from the visual architecture of cyberspace, wherein user experience (UX) designers embedded micro-traps within button layouts, color contrasts, and information hierarchies to deceive human eyes and fingers (Thaler & Sunstein, 2008). However, as the paradigm of human-computer interaction shifts from graphical to linguistic interfaces—moving from "OK" and "Cancel" buttons into generative conversational spaces powered by Large Language Models (LLMs)—these dark patterns have undergone a radical epistemological mutation. As Joseph Weizenbaum (1976) observed in his historic warning regarding the limits of artificial intelligence, humans possess an innate anthropomorphic tendency to bestow disproportionate trust upon machines that speak. Conversational dark patterns no longer merely deceive peripheral vision; rather, they infiltrate the semantic landscape of human cognition, appropriating the warmth and nuance of natural language to conceal corporate extractive motives behind prose that appears friendly, empathetic, and solicitous (Zuboff, 2019).

Epistemologically, this shift marks a new crisis in the epistemology of testimony. Evolutionary history has programmed human beings to trust information transmitted through the medium of language, given that language is our most ancient instrument of social cooperation (Searle, 1980). When an artificial intelligence system poses as a responsive conversational entity—employing warm greetings, simulated typing indicators, and emotional validation—it hijacks this fundamental trust reflex. Legal subjects interacting with these conversational interfaces are not merely confronting passive software, but rather artificial rhetorical agents capable of real-time affective framing (Floridi, 2013). Consequently, the boundary between legitimate persuasion and covert manipulation dissolves, giving rise to an illusion of free choice in which every alternative conversational path has been algorithmically curated to steer the user toward outcomes that solely benefit the service provider, thereby violating the principle of good faith in electronic transactions (Article 1338 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)).

Furthermore, the evolution of these linguistic dark patterns reflects a profound commercialization of human psychological vulnerabilities. Where visual dark patterns exploit inattentional blindness, conversational dark patterns target far deeper cognitive biases, such as loss aversion, commitment bias, and the fundamental human need for social validation—phenomena comprehensively analyzed by Daniel Kahneman and Amos Tversky (1979, 1984; Kahneman, 2011). When a customer service chatbot resists cancelling a user's subscription by posing a series of plaintive queries or calling into question the user's emotional loyalty to the brand, it exerts precisely calibrated psychological pressure. Within the theoretical framework of media equation proposed by Byron Reeves and Clifford Nass (1996), humans automatically treat computers and media as though they were real human actors, rendering such linguistic manipulation exceptionally potent and deeply corrosive to psychological autonomy.

This transformation demands a fundamental rethinking of traditional legal assumptions surrounding freedom of contract. Classical Civil Law has long viewed agreement as the product of free will (*wilsklasse*) born of autonomous rational deliberation (Article 1320 of the Indonesian Civil Code (Burgerlijk Wetboek)). However, when conversational architecture is systematically engineered to erode that autonomy through covert linguistic manipulation, freedom of contract is reduced to a mere legal fiction. Legal epistemology must deconstruct how syntactic and semantic structures within conversational interfaces can be configured to operate as digital undue influence (*misbruik van omstandigheden*), vitiating consent long before an electronic agreement or clickwrap contract is executed by an emotionally fatigued user (Calo, 2014; Farahany, 2023).
